newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end lower after rally fails.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end lower after rally fails.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended lower Tuesday, on moderate volumes, after an early rally in gold and silver failed to convincingly breach three week old resistance, amid talk of more European central bank activity, traders said.
But NYMEX platinum and palladium futures remained well supported, with the physical market still very tight, refining sources said.

"COMEX June gold has held above its contract low at $339.50 for three weeks now, and took out a little bit of resistance above $345.00 today, but there was no follow through, and gold just fell back toward the bottom of the range," said Scott Myers, senior analyst with Pioneer Futures in New York.
COMEX June gold ended down $2.80 an ounce at $341.50, after rallying to a session high early at $345.50 on light fund and bullion bank buying.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $340.30/80, compared with the London Tuesday afternoon fix at $342.45 and the New York close Monday around $342.50/00.
COMEX June gold has been trapped in a $340.00-345.00 range since mid-April, with traders advocating buying call and put option combinations to take advantage of range breakout.

With the downtrend losing momentum, funds been covering some short positions, analysts said. COMEX gold open interest fell 1,125 lots Monday to 166,239 contracts, reflecting the fund shortcovering, traders said.

News Monday that the Bre-X deposit in Busang Indonesia was non-existent, meant an expected 71 million ounces of mine supply would not now be coming to market, and helped to provide gold prices with some support also, traders said.

But "the prospect of hedge and central bank sales are acting as a depressant on gold and the absence of inflationary pressure is a negative for the (precious metals) group," Bear Stearns senior analyst Bill Byers said.

Some bullion bankers admit there has been some derivative-based central bank activity in recent weeks, and there have been unconfirmed rumors the Dutch central bank has again been mobilizing its gold reserves.
In January the Dutch central bank confirmed selling about 300 tonnes of gold in late 1996, but on April 22 a Dutch central bank spokesman denied the bank was active currently.

Analysts argue European central banks are keen to convert their gold reserves into income earning assets ahead of the introduction of European Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999, as they will lose control of their gold reserves from that date.
The planned European central bank (ECB) will make an initial call on EMU countries to contribute about $67 billion, mainly in the form of dollars and gold, to ECB reserves.

But remaining gold and currency reserves held by existing European central banks will then remain at the call of the ECB, meaning EMU countries will have lost their opportunity to convert gold reserves into income earning assets.
European central banks hold about 14,000 tonnes (450 million ounces) of gold, over 40 percent of all official world gold reserves.

The spot gold/silver ratio remained little changed around 72:1, with COMEX July silver ending down 3.5 cents at $4.733 an ounce, after the contract ran into resistance at $4.790, near the top of its three week old range.
NYMEX July platinum ended down 10 cents at $373.00, while NYMEX June palladium lost $1.70 to end at $156.20.

But, in the absence of any sign of a resumption of Russian platinum group metal (PGM) exports, PGM lease rates remain very high, near-month palladium prices remain in backwardation, and physical market prices remain above futures market prices, analysts noted.
"The practice of using long-term supply contracts by the automotive and electronics industries has dampened volatility in the platinum group," Byers said.
But "the interesting story for the group is the attempt by Russia to support platinum prices via export restrictions."
